2.text: Indighirka tundra, etc., still take care that each of their camps, corresponding

3.text: to a separate herd, shall have as front-house master one of their nearest relatives.

4.text: With Eiˊheli each herd was looked after by an adult son; and the sons were

5.text: almost the real possessors of the herd, from the very beginning of their

6.text: independent life. One of them, for instance, in order to avoid being controlled

7.text: in any way by the father, wandered with the herd into the distant mountains,

8.text: and did not appear in the father’s vicinity for three consecutive years. When

9.text: I was with Eiˊheli, the old man sometimes felt angry about it, and grumbled,

10.text: “I will go there and take away my herd.” We knew, however, that he was

11.text: of a boastful disposition, and liked to exaggerate the extent of his force and

12.text: influence. All the people about him were quite sure that, even if he should

13.text: go and find the reprobate son, he would not think of taking the herd from

14.text: him, nor would he be able to do so. With Omrêlqoˊt, two herds of his were

15.text: under the direction of his two wives, and the younger brother of Omrêlqoˊt

16.text: cared for the third. The same was the case with Araˊro and the others.

17.text: So, when Maydell mentions, in the words of Amraˊwkurg̣ɪn, that with the

18.text: rich Chukchee the herds are usually given to the assistants, who live with

19.text: them quite independent of the master, slaughter and sell animals, and that

20.text: the only condition of their contract is that the herd must be kept in good

21.text: health and must multiply in number,¹ I can only attribute it to a complete

22.text: misunderstanding. The herd cannot exist without the special charms, the ear-

23.text: mark, anointing-mark, etc., of its owner’s family, all of which are necessary

24.text: for good-luck. And no family will trust its “reindeer-luck” to a stranger, or,

25.text: what is still worse, will suffer its sacred belongings to be replaced by those of

26.text: another family. All the conditions of life of the Reindeer Chukchee are such,

27.text: that an assistant who would live by himself with a herd, after a few years

28.text: would become master of this herd no matter to whom it originally belonged.

29.text: Still more difficult to understand are the communications of Maydell con-

30.text: cerning the aristocracy among the Reindeer Chukchee, founded on the different

31.text: sizes of their herds.² No trace of such a thing actually exists. Maydell’s

32.text: opinion may be explained only by his position as a Russian official, who

33.text: endeavored by every means to create “chiefs” and authority among the savage

34.text: Chukchee. I will speak of this later in more detail.

35.text: Kuvaˊr of Indian Point, being an Eskimo, and therefore having no rein-

36.text: deer-herd of his own, actually bought a quantity of reindeer and gave them

37.text: all to a Chukchee friend of his. This herd, however, cannot be compared

38.text: with the usual herds. The animals were all acquired by purchase, and, to

39.text: speak correctly, this herd formed the product of trade with the Americans.

40.text: Moreover, Kuvaˊr was content to receive from the herd a certain amount of

41.text: meat and skins, and did not look too closely into the dealings of his manager.

42.text: Assistants of Alien Origin. — In those parts of the Chukchee territory
